description_full: Rollins, Inc., through its subsidiaries, provides pest and wildlife control services and protection to residential and commercial customers in the United States and internationally. The company offers pest control services to residential properties protecting from common pests, including rodents, insects, and wildlife. It also provides workplace pest control solutions for customers across various end markets, such as healthcare, food service, and logistics. In addition, the company offers termite protection and ancillary services for both residential and commercial customers. It serves clients directly, as well as through franchisee operations. The company was formerly known as Rollins Broadcasting, Inc and changed its name to Rollins, Inc. in 1965. Rollins, Inc. was founded in 1901 and is headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia.

financial_summary: Rollins, Inc. is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $18.3B market cap on $3.8B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +12% over the past three years and +10% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 36% against a 8% cost of capital — a 28-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $650M in free cash flow — roughly 17 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.29× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.6× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 25× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 3.0% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 39% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 2.3× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 19% operating margin runs 12pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (8%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 2.34x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 48% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has rebounded 6% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 43% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 29% and a beta of 0.65, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $203.9M traded a day, and interest is running hot at 1.7x its yearly average volume.
In past sell-offs it fell 22% in the 2020 crash, 15% in the 2022 bear market and 37% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $22.43 (margin of safety -69%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 13%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $17.65 to $29.04 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 34.8 vs 19.3, EV/EBITDA 22.5 vs 11.2 and P/FCF 28.1 vs 16.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 25% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.6% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 3.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 17 covering analysts target $37.24 on average, 2% below the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 36% clears the cost of capital of 7.9% by 28pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.13).
It converts 17% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.29x.
ROE of 38% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.3x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.1% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.6x net debt to EBITDA ($100.0M of cash against $609.8M of debt), with interest covered 25.4x.
The current ratio of 0.60 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
Goodwill makes up 44% of assets, a soft asset exposed to impairment.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 11.7% over 3 years, 11.7% over 5 years and 9.7% over 10 years.
Net reinvestment is nil (capex and working capital no more than cover depreciation), so fundamental growth is near zero.
Free cash flow has compounded 9.5% a year over five years.
Capex runs only 0.2x depreciation (0.7% of sales), so the asset base is being harvested rather than grown.
Its Rule of 40 score is 28, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 39.1%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 62%.
Insider trading is two-way: 2 purchases and 1 sale over the past year, net $99.1M bought.
It returns 3.0% a year to shareholders (1.2% in buybacks and 2.1% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 0.6% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 39 consecutive years, raising it 15.4% a year over the last five.
people: With about 22,000 employees, each generates about $171K of revenue, 0.4x the Consumer Cyclical median, and productivity has risen 8.3% a year.
That works out to $30K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.8M (17x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (9/10, lower is better).
